en: Saṃyutta Nikāya 9.1 (SN 9.1, SN 221, PTS [1st ed. SN i 197, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 424) 1. Vanavagga Vivekasutta (Seclusion) “Bhikkhus, there are these five aggregates subject to clinging. What five? The form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the volitional formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. When a bhikkhu has seen with wisdom as they really are the origin and the passing away of these five aggregates subject to clinging, he is called a bhikkhu who dwells in seclusion, who delights in seclusion, who finds satisfaction in seclusion, who is devoted to seclusion, who is intent on seclusion, who is committed to seclusion, who is dedicated to seclusion, who is resolved upon seclusion, who is bent toward seclusion, who is inclined toward seclusion, who is disposed toward seclusion, who is bound for seclusion, who is headed for seclusion, who is destined for seclusion, who is one whose destination is seclusion, who is one whose final end is seclusion, who is one whose ultimate goal is seclusion, who is one whose final conclusion is seclusion, who is one whose final limit is seclusion, who is one whose final resort is seclusion, who is one whose final rest is seclusion, who is one whose final abode is seclusion, who is one whose final refuge is seclusion, who is one whose final liberation is seclusion. And what, bhikkhus, is seclusion? It is the complete destruction, fading away, cessation, stilling, and disappearance of lust, hatred, and delusion.”
Thus have I heard:
at one time a certain bhikkhu was dwelling among the Kosalans in a certain forest grove.
Now on that occasion, having gone for his midday rest, that bhikkhu was thinking evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with worldly attachment.

Then a deity dwelling in that forest grove, who was compassionate and well-wishing toward that bhikkhu and desiring to stir him to spiritual urgency, approached that bhikkhu. Having approached, she addressed that bhikkhu in verse:
“You have entered the forest desiring seclusion, yet you are not practicing seclusion.”
Now your mind wanders outward;
subdue your desire for people among people,
and then you will be happy, free from passion.
Mindful, you abandoned discontent;
we remind you of that which is mindful for the virtuous.
For the dust of the underworld is indeed difficult to cross.
Let not the dust of sensual desire carry you away,
just as a bird covered in dirt shakes off and sheds the dust clinging to it.
“Thus, a bhikkhu who is diligent and mindful shakes off and casts away the dust that clings to him.
Then that bhikkhu, stirred by that deity, experienced a sense of spiritual urgency.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 9.2 (SN 9.2, SN 222, PTS [1st ed. SN i 197, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 425) 1. Vanavagga Upaṭṭhānasutta At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, when one thing is present, ignorance comes to be; with the arising of that one thing, ignorance arises. What one thing? Contact. When this one thing—contact—is present, ignorance comes to be; with the arising of this one thing—contact—ignorance arises. When one thing is present, craving comes to be; with the arising of that one thing, craving arises. What one thing? Contact. When this one thing—contact—is present, craving comes to be; with the arising of this one thing—contact—craving arises. When one thing is present, feeling comes to be; with the arising of that one thing, feeling arises. What one thing? Contact. When this one thing—contact—is present, feeling comes to be; with the arising of this one thing—contact—feeling arises. When one thing is present, perception comes to be; with the arising of that one thing, perception arises. What one thing? Contact. When this one thing—contact—is present, perception comes to be; with the arising of this one thing—contact—perception arises. When one thing is present, volitional formations come to be; with the arising of that one thing, volitional formations arise. What one thing? Contact. When this one thing—contact—is present, volitional formations come to be; with the arising of this one thing—contact—volitional formations arise. “Bhikkhus, when one thing is absent, ignorance does not come to be; with the cessation of that one thing, ignorance ceases. When this one thing—contact—is absent, feeling does not come to be; with the cessation of this one thing—contact—feeling ceases. When this one thing—contact—is absent, perception does not come to be; with the cessation of this one thing—contact—perception ceases. When one thing is absent, volitional formations do not come to be; with the cessation of that one thing, volitional formations cease. What one thing? Contact. On one occasion, a certain bhikkhu was dwelling among the Kosalans in a certain forest grove.
Now on that occasion, having gone there for his midday rest, that bhikkhu was sleeping.
Then the deity who inhabited that forest grove, being compassionate and desiring his welfare, [approached him].
Desiring to stir that bhikkhu, they approached him; having approached, they addressed that bhikkhu with verses:
“Arise, bhikkhu! Why do you lie there?
What is the use of your sleeping?
For what sleep can there be for one who is afflicted,
pierced by arrows, and suffering?
That very faith through which one has gone forth—
From the home to the homeless life—
cultivate that very faith;
do not fall under the power of sloth.”
“Sensual pleasures are impermanent and unstable,
in which even a fool is infatuated;
they are like being released from bonds while still bound, or like eating what is inedible.”
Why would one torment one who has gone forth?
Through the subduing of desire and lust,
and through the transcendence of ignorance.
That knowledge is supremely pure;
why would it afflict one who has gone forth?
Having cut off ignorance with true knowledge, [one is free].
Through the complete destruction of the taints,
he has reached sorrowlessness and freedom from distress;
why, then, should one afflict one who has gone forth?
One who has aroused energy, is resolute,
and is constantly firm in effort,
longing for Nibbāna—
“Why do you torment one who has gone forth?
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 9.3 (Vanavagga)
The Discourse to Kassapagotta.
On one occasion the Venerable Kassapagotta was living among the Kosalans in a certain woodland thicket.
Now at that time, while the Venerable Kassapagotta had gone for his midday rest, he was instructing a certain fowler.
Then a deity dwelling in that forest grove, desiring to stir the Venerable Kassapagotta, approached the Venerable Kassapagotta;
having approached, she addressed the Venerable Kassapagotta in verses:
“This fowl who wanders through the mountain fastnesses—”
To one who is without conceptual proliferation and without mind,
a monk who exhorts at an improper time seems dull to me.
He hears but does not discern;
he looks but does not see,
while the Dhamma is being recited.
The fool does not understand the goal.
Even if you were to hold ten lamps, Kassapa;
“He will not see forms,
for his eye does not exist.
Then the Venerable Kassapagotta, stirred by that deity, experienced a sense of spiritual urgency.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 9.4 (SN 9.4, SN 224, PTS [1st ed. SN i 199, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 428) 1. Vanavagga Sambahulasutta At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then a number of bhikkhus approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to him: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach us the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, we might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “Bhikkhus, if you should dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, then this will be for you a brief exposition of the Dhamma: ‘All phenomena are non-self. When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But how, venerable sir, is it that all phenomena are non-self? “Whatever is felt, bhikkhu, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all that is non-self. This, bhikkhu, is how it is that all phenomena are non-self. When this was said, another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But how, venerable sir, does one know, how does one see, so that in regard to this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena, there is no I-making, mine-making, or underlying tendency to conceit? “Whatever is felt, bhikkhu, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all that is felt should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. When one sees it thus as it really is with correct wisdom, bhikkhu, then in regard to this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena, there is no I-making, mine-making, or underlying tendency to conceit. When this was said, yet another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But how, venerable sir, is there the cessation of I-making, mine-making, and the underlying tendency to conceit? “When, bhikkhu, one does not cling to anything in the world, does not take a stand upon anything in the world, then there is no I-making, mine-making, or underlying tendency to conceit. When this was said, yet another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But how, venerable sir, does one know, how does one see, so that one does not cling to anything in the world or take a stand upon anything in the world? “Whatever is seen, bhikkhu, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, or pondered by the intellect—when one does not cling to that, does not take a stand upon that, then one does not cling to anything in the world or take a stand upon anything in the world. When this was said, yet another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But how, venerable sir, does one know, how does one see, so that one does not cling to anything seen, heard, sensed, or cognized; so that one does not take a stand upon anything attained, sought after, or pondered by the intellect? “Whatever is seen, bhikkhu, is seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. Whatever is heard... sensed... cognized is cognized as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. When one sees it thus as it really is with correct wisdom, bhikkhu, then one does not cling to anything seen, heard, sensed, or cognized; then one does not take a stand upon anything attained, sought after, or pondered by the intellect. When this was said, yet another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But how, venerable sir, does one know, how does one see, so that one does not cling to anything seen, heard, sensed, or cognized; so that one does not take a stand upon anything attained, sought after, or pondered by the intellect? “Whatever is seen, bhikkhu, is seen as empty of self and of what belongs to self. Whatever is heard... sensed... cognized is cognized as empty of self and of what belongs to self. When one sees it thus as it really is with correct wisdom, bhikkhu, then one does not cling to anything seen, heard, sensed, or cognized; then one does not take a stand upon anything attained, sought after, or pondered by the intellect. When this was said, yet another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But how, venerable sir, does one know, how does one see, so that one does not cling to anything seen, heard, sensed, or cognized; so that one does not take a stand upon anything attained, sought after, or pondered by the intellect? “Whatever is seen, bhikkhu, is seen as impermanent. Whatever is heard... sensed... cognized is cognized as impermanent. When one sees it thus as it really is with correct wisdom, bhikkhu, then one does not cling to anything seen, heard, sensed, or cognized; then one does not take a stand upon anything attained, sought after, or pondered by the intellect. When this was said, yet another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But how, venerable sir, does one know, how does one see, so that one does not cling to anything seen, heard, sensed, or cognized; so that one does not take a stand upon anything attained, sought after, or pondered by the intellect? “Whatever is seen, bhikkhu, is seen as suffering. Whatever is heard... sensed... cognized is cognized as suffering. When one sees it thus as it really is with correct wisdom, bhikkhu, then one does not cling to anything seen, heard, sensed, or cognized; then one does not take a stand upon anything attained, sought after, or pondered by the intellect. When this was said, yet another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But how, venerable sir, does one know, how does one see, so that one does not cling to anything seen, heard, sensed, or cognized; so that one does not take a stand upon anything attained, sought after, or pondered by the intellect? “Whatever is seen, bhikkhu, is seen as non-self. Whatever is heard... sensed... cognized is cognized as non-self.

When one sees it thus as it really is with correct wisdom, bhikkhu, then one does not cling to anything seen, heard, sensed, or cognized; then one does not take a stand upon anything attained, sought after, or pondered by the intellect. When this was said, yet another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But how, venerable sir, does one know, how does one see, so that one does not cling to anything seen, heard, sensed, or cognized; so that one does not take a stand upon anything attained, sought after, or pondered by the intellect? “Whatever is seen, bhikkhu, is seen as subject to arising. Whatever is heard... sensed... cognized is cognized as subject to arising. When one sees it thus as it really is with correct wisdom, bhikkhu, then one does not cling to anything seen, heard, sensed, or cognized; then one does not take a stand upon anything attained, sought after, or pondered by the intellect. When this was said, yet another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But how, venerable sir, does one know, how does one see, so that one does not cling to anything seen, heard, sensed, or cognized; so that one does not take a stand upon anything attained, sought after, or pondered by the intellect? “Whatever is seen, bhikkhu, is seen as subject to vanishing. Whatever is heard... sensed... cognized is cognized as subject to vanishing. When one sees it thus as it really is with correct wisdom, bhikkhu, then one does not cling to anything seen, heard, sensed, or cognized; then one does not take a stand upon anything attained, sought after, or pondered by the intellect. When this was said, yet another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But how, venerable sir, does one know, how does one see, so that one does not cling to anything seen, heard, sensed, or cognized; so that one does not take a stand upon anything attained, sought after, or pondered by the intellect? “Whatever is seen, bhikkhu, is seen as subject to cessation. Whatever is heard... sensed... cognized is cognized as subject to cessation. When one sees it thus as it really is with correct wisdom, bhikkhu, then one does not cling to anything seen, heard, sensed, or cognized; then one does not take a stand upon anything attained, sought after, or pondered by the intellect
On one occasion, a number of bhikkhus were dwelling among the Kosalans in a certain forest grove.
Then, having completed the rains retreat at the end of the three months, those bhikkhus set out on a journey.
Thereupon, the deity who inhabited that forest grove, not seeing those bhikkhus, lamenting at that time, spoke this verse:
“Seeing many secluded seats, one who is dissatisfied appears as if possessed by a demon;
those who are eloquent and learned in speech— ”
“Where have the disciples of Gotama gone?
When this was said, a certain deity replied to that deity in verse:
“They have gone to Magadha; they have gone to Kosala.”
But some bhikkhus in the Vajjian country dwell without a fixed abode, moving about unattached like deer.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 9.5 (SN 9.5, SN 225, PTS [1st ed. SN i 199, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 429) 1. Vanavagga Ānanda Sutta At Sāvatthī. There, the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, this forest is delightful, this forest is beautiful, this forest is secluded from noise, free from the sound of people, remote, suitable for seclusion. It is here that those bhikkhus who are arahants, whose taints are destroyed, who have lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached their own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and are liberated through final knowledge, would dwell delighting in the bliss of liberation. It is here that those bhikkhus who are non-returners, with the five lower fetters destroyed, would dwell, having completely transcended the plane of sense-sphere beings. It is here that those bhikkhus who are once-returners, with three fetters destroyed and with greed, hatred, and delusion weakened, would dwell, having returned only once more to this world to make an end of suffering. It is here that those bhikkhus who are stream-enterers, possessing unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, would dwell, having entered the fixed course of rightness and being assured of full enlightenment. It is here that those bhikkhus who are practicing for the realization of the fruit of arahantship would dwell, having abandoned the five lower fetters. It is here that those bhikkhus who are practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-return would dwell, having abandoned the five lower fetters. It is here that those bhikkhus who are practicing for the realization of the fruit of once-return would dwell, having abandoned three fetters and weakened greed, hatred, and delusion. It is here that those bhikkhus who are practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry would dwell, having abandoned three fetters. It is here that those bhikkhus who are practicing for the attainment of the first jhāna would dwell, having abandoned the five hindrances, those defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom. It is here that those bhikkhus who are practicing for the attainment of the second jhāna would dwell, having stilled applied and sustained thought. It is here that those bhikkhus who are practicing for the attainment of the third jhāna would dwell, having made zest fade away. It is here that those bhikkhus who are practicing for the attainment of the fourth jhāna would dwell, having abandoned pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, having entered and dwelling in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity. It is here that those bhikkhus who are practicing for the attainment of the base of infinite space would dwell, having completely transcended forms, with the passing away of perceptions of sensory impact, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, thinking, ‘Space is infinite. It is here that those bhikkhus who are practicing for the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness would dwell, having completely transcended the base of infinite space, thinking, ‘Consciousness is infinite. It is here that those bhikkhus who are practicing for the attainment of the base of nothingness would dwell, having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness, thinking, ‘There is nothing. It is here that those bhikkhus who are practicing for the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception would dwell, having completely transcended the base of nothingness. It is here that those bhikkhus who are practicing for the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling would dwell, having completely transcended the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and through the total stilling of perceptions and feelings, having entered and dwelling in the cessation of perception and feeling. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, venerable sir, it is marvelous! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘This forest is delightful... and so on, up to ‘...having entered and dwelling in the cessation of perception and feeling. “Indeed, Ānanda, this forest is delightful, this forest is beautiful, this forest is secluded from noise, free from the sound of people, remote, suitable for seclusion. It is here that those bhikkhus who are arahants... would dwell delighting in the bliss of liberation. It is here that those bhikkhus who are practicing for the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling would dwell, having completely transcended the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and through the total stilling of perceptions and feelings, having entered and dwelling in the cessation of perception and feeling. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is as if a man were to seek out a hidden treasure of gold, and having found it, were to sit down and say: ‘This is where my hidden treasure of gold is; I have found it. Even so, venerable sir, it is as if I were to seek out the Dhamma-treasure hidden by the Tathāgata, and having found it, were to sit down and say: ‘This is where the Dhamma-treasure hidden by the Blessed One is; I have found it. “It is wonderful, Ānanda, it is marvelous how well you have grasped the meaning of what was briefly stated by me! Thus spoke the Blessed One. Elated, the Venerable Ānanda rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One. (This concludes the fifth discourse in the Forest Chapter.)
On one occasion the Venerable Ānanda was dwelling among the Kosalans in a certain forest grove.
Now at that time, the Venerable Ānanda was spending excessive time occupied with socializing with householders.
Then a deity who dwelt in that forest grove, out of compassion for the Venerable Ānanda and desiring his welfare, [approached him...]
Desiring to stir the Venerable Ānanda, she approached him and, having approached,
addressed the Venerable Ānanda in verse:
“Having gone to the thicket at the foot of a tree...”
“Having placed Nibbāna within your heart, meditate, Gotama; do not be negligent!
What will that rattling sound do for you?”
Then the Venerable Ānanda, stirred by that deity, experienced a sense of spiritual urgency.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 9.6 (SN 9.6, SN 226, PTS [1st ed. SN i 200, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 430) 1.
Vanavagga (The Forest Chapter)
The Discourse to Anuruddha On one occasion the Venerable Anuruddha was dwelling among the Kosalans in a certain forest grove.

Then a certain deity from the Tāvatiṃsa host named Jālinī, who had formerly been the Venerable Anuruddha’s wife, approached the Venerable Anuruddha. Having approached, she addressed the Venerable Anuruddha in verse:
“Direct your mind there,
to where you formerly dwelt:
among the Tāvatiṃsa gods.”
Amidst the fulfillment of all desires,
honored and surrounded by celestial maidens, you shine forth in splendor.”
“Wretched are the daughters of the gods,
established in a self-identity;
and those beings, too, are wretched.”
“Those who do not see the Nandana grove do not understand happiness, for it is longed for by the daughters of the gods.”
“The abode of the gods among men,
of the glorious Thirty-Three.
“You do not understand, you fool!”
Just as is the word of the Arahants:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent,
subject to the nature of arising and passing away."
Having arisen, they cease;
their subsiding is blissful.
There is now no further dwelling.
In the net-like host of gods,
the wandering through births is exhausted;
there is now no further existence.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 9.7 (SN 9.7, SN 227, PTS [1st ed. SN i 200, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 432) 1. Vanavagga Nāgadattasutta At Sāvatthī. There, the Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, when one thing is developed and cultivated, it leads to a great result and great benefit. What is that one thing? It is loving-kindness meditation (*mettābhāvanā*). When loving-kindness meditation is developed and cultivated, it leads to a great result and great benefit. “Suppose, bhikkhus, there were a great tree standing possessed of heartwood. A man would come along needing heartwood. He would cut down the great tree at its foot and, having cut it down, he would take out the heartwood and go off with it. Then another man would come along needing heartwood. He would cut down the great tree at its foot and, having cut it down, he would take out the heartwood and go off with it. On one occasion the Venerable Nāgadatta was dwelling among the Kosalans in a certain forest grove.
Now at that time, the Venerable Nāgadatta would enter the village too early and return from it too late.
Then a deity who dwelt in that forest grove, being compassionate and desiring his welfare, [addressed him].
Desiring to stir the venerable Nāgadatta to spiritual urgency, she approached the venerable Nāgadatta;
having approached him, she addressed the venerable Nāgadatta in verses:
“Enter at the proper time, Nāgadatta;”
Coming during the day, he wanders about excessively;
he socializes with householders,
sharing in their joys and sorrows.
I fear Nāgadatta, who is so arrogant and bound by his attachment to his clans;
may he not fall into the power of the mighty King of Death.
“...he fell under the power of the Ender.
Then the Venerable Nāgadatta, stirred by that deity, experienced a sense of spiritual urgency.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya 9.8 (SN 9.8, SN 228, PTS [1st ed. SN i 201; PTS [2nd ed. SN i 433)*
1. The Chapter on Forests (Vanavagga). Discourse on the Housewife of a Noble Family (Kulagharaṇīsutta).
At one time, a certain bhikkhu was dwelling among the Kosalans in a certain forest grove.
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu was staying for too long, having become deeply immersed in a particular family.
Then a deity dwelling in that forest grove, who was compassionate and well-wishing toward that bhikkhu and desiring to stir him with a sense of urgency,
manifested herself in the form of the mistress of that family.
He approached that bhikkhu and, having approached, addressed him with a verse:
“On the banks of rivers,
in gathering places, in assembly halls, and on the streets;”
"People gather and deliberate;
what is the difference between me and them?
"Many voices are in opposition."
An ascetic should be patient;
he should not be dejected by that,
for he is not defiled by it.
But he who is one who relies on the protection of faith is like a deer in the wind in the forest;
him they call "light-minded."
“His vow does not succeed.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 9.9 (SN 9.9, SN 229, PTS [1st ed. SN i 201; PTS [2nd ed. SN i 434) 1. Vanavagga (The Chapter on the Forest)
The Discourse to the Vajjiputtaka:
On one occasion a certain monk who was a Vajjiputtaka was staying at Vesālī in a certain grove.
Now at that time, there was a Vajjiputtaka in Vesālī who was a night-wanderer.
Then that bhikkhu, having heard the sound of the noise of musical instruments, cymbals, and drums in Vesālī, lamenting at that time, spoke this verse:
“We dwell alone in the forest like a piece of wood cast away in the woods.”
"On such a night as this,
who indeed could be more wretched than we? Then,
the deity dwelling in that forest thicket, out of compassion and wishing for his welfare, [spoke].
Desiring to stir that bhikkhu to spiritual urgency, they approached him; having approached, they addressed that bhikkhu with a verse:
"You dwell alone in the forest like a piece of wood cast away in the woods."
"Many envy you, just as those bound for hell envy one going to heaven.
Then that bhikkhu, stirred by that deity, experienced a sense of spiritual urgency.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 9.10 The Chapter on Forests (Vanavagga) Sajjhāya Sutta: Recitation At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is one who recites the Dhamma, he should do so with reference to three things. What three? ‘This Dhamma is for the sake of disenchantment with all formations; it is for the sake of dispassion toward them, for their fading away, and for their cessation. When a bhikkhu is one who recites the Dhamma, he should do so with reference to these three things.”

Now at that time, that bhikkhu—who had previously spent an excessive amount of time occupied with recitation—was on a later occasion dwelling indifferently, silent, and withdrawn. Then a deity who dwelt in that forest grove, not hearing the Dhamma from that bhikkhu, approached him; having approached, she addressed that bhikkhu in verse: [The deity said: "Formerly you were intent on recitation, But now you dwell indifferent and silent. “Why, O bhikkhu, though living in the company of bhikkhus, do you not recite the verses of the Dhamma?
Having heard the Dhamma, one gains serene confidence.”
"One receives praise even in this very life.
"In former times there was a longing for the verses on Dhamma,
until we came to encounter dispassion."
"Since we have come together through dispassion regarding whatever is seen, heard, or sensed,
the virtuous say that it is by means of final knowledge that one lays down [the burden]."

Saṁyutta Nikāya 9.11 The Discourse on Unwholesome Thoughts (1. Vanavagga) At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, there are these three unwholesome thoughts. What three? The thought of sensual desire, the thought of ill will, and the thought of cruelty.
These, bhikkhus, are the three unwholesome thoughts.”
On one occasion, a certain bhikkhu was dwelling among the Kosalans in a certain forest grove.
Now at that time, having gone for his midday rest, that bhikkhu was thinking evil, unwholesome thoughts, namely:
thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of cruelty.

Then a deity dwelling in that forest grove, who was compassionate and well-wishing toward that bhikkhu and desiring to stir him to spiritual urgency, approached that bhikkhu; having approached, she addressed that bhikkhu in verses:
“From improper attention, ...”
Thus you are devoured by discursive thoughts;
relinquish improper reflection and reflect with proper wisdom.
Taking as your object the Teacher, the Dhamma,
the Saṅgha, and your own virtues,
you attain gladness.
“Without doubt, there is joy and happiness;
from that, abounding in gladness,
you will make an end of suffering.”
Then that bhikkhu, stirred by that deity, experienced a sense of spiritual urgency.

The Midday Discourse.
On one occasion, a certain bhikkhu was dwelling among the Kosalans in a certain forest grove.
Then a deity dwelling in that forest grove approached that bhikkhu; having approached, she recited this verse in his presence:
“At the time of midday,
when the birds have settled down,
the great forest seems as if it were silent.”
That fear appears to me:
when midday has arrived and the birds have settled down.
"The vast forest rustles;
that delight appears to my mind.
— *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 9.13 (SN 9.13, SN 233, PTS [1st ed. SN i 203, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 438)
1. The Chapter on Forests:

The Discourse on Those with Unrestrained Faculties On one occasion, a number of bhikkhus were dwelling among the Kosalans in a certain forest grove; they were restless, arrogant, fickle, talkative, loose-tongued, muddled in mindfulness, lacking clear comprehension, unconcentrated, with wandering minds, and with unrestrained faculties.

Then a deity dwelling in that forest grove, who was compassionate toward those bhikkhus, desiring their welfare, and wishing to stir them to spiritual urgency, approached those bhikkhus; having approached, she addressed those bhikkhus in verses:
“In former times they lived happily...”
The monks are disciples of Gotama;
they seek alms without desire,
and they dwell in lodgings without desire.
Having understood impermanence in the world,
they brought an end to suffering;
having made themselves difficult to satisfy, they attained peace.
Like village headmen in a village,
they lie down after eating again and again,
infatuated with the houses of others.
Having joined my palms in reverence to the Sangha,
I speak here to certain people:
they are cast away and without a protector.
Just as the hungry ghosts are,
so too are they. It was with reference to those who dwell negligently that I spoke this.
“Homage to those who dwell with diligence;
to them I pay homage.
Then those bhikkhus, stirred by that deity, were moved to a sense of spiritual urgency.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 9.14 (SN 9.14, SN 234, PTS [1st ed. SN i 204, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 440) 1. Vanavagga Gandhatthenasutta (The Thief of Fragrance) At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, suppose a thief were to steal a fragrant flower from its stalk. Then a second thief would come along and steal that fragrant flower from the first thief. Then a third thief would come along and steal that fragrant flower from the second thief. Then a fourth thief would come along and steal that fragrant flower from the third thief. Now, bhikkhus, which of these four thieves would be the one who has stolen the fragrant flower? “Venerable sir, the one who stole it from the stalk. “But, bhikkhus, the one who stole it from the stalk is still far away from the fragrant flower. The one who stole it from him is closer; the one who stole it from him is closer still; and the one who stole it from him is even closer. But the one who wears the fragrant flower on his head or on his ear—that one is the very pinnacle of those who have stolen the fragrant flower. “So too, bhikkhus, there are these five cords of sensual pleasure. What five? Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, sensually enticing, tantalizing. Sounds cognizable by the ear... Odors cognizable by the nose... Tastes cognizable by the tongue... Tactile objects cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, sensually enticing, tantalizing. These are the five cords of sensual pleasure. “Now, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu has not abandoned lust for these five cords of sensual pleasure, he is called a ‘thief of fragrance’ in the Noble One’s Discipline. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, this is a designation for the five cords of sensual pleasure: ‘fragrance,’ I say, is a designation for the five cords of sensual pleasure. And the Noble Ones, I say, do not consort with anyone who is a thief of fragrance. “But when a bhikkhu has abandoned lust for these five cords of sensual pleasure, he is called one who does not steal fragrance in the Noble One’s Discipline. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, this is a designation for the five cords of sensual pleasure: ‘fragrance,’ I say, is a designation for the five cords of sensual pleasure. And the Noble Ones, I say, consort with one who does not steal fragrance.”
On one occasion, a certain bhikkhu was dwelling among the Kosalans in a certain forest grove.
Now at that time, after his meal, having returned from his almsround, that bhikkhu had plunged into a lotus pond and was sniffing a lotus.
Then, the deity who dwelt in that forest grove, out of compassion for that bhikkhu and desiring his welfare—
Desiring to stir that bhikkhu, they approached him; having approached, they addressed that bhikkhu with a verse:
“This water-born flower which you smell, though it was not given to you;”
“This is one factor of thefts:
you are a thief of fragrance, dear sir.
“I do not take, nor do I break;”
I smell the water-born lotus from afar;
by what quality, then,
is it called a "thief of fragrance"?
He who digs up lotus roots and breaks off white lotuses—
thus is one whose actions are defiled.
"Why is this not said?
[The answer is: "A man who is greedy and full of defilement is like a soiled nurse’s cloth."
I have no word for him,
yet you are worthy to speak;
for a person free from blemish—
For one who constantly seeks purity,
even a hair’s tip of evil appears as large as a cloud.”
“Surely you know me, O yakkha,
and you have compassion for me;
speak to me again, O yakkha.”
"When you see such as this," [he said].
"We do not depend on you for our livelihood,
nor are we your hired servants."
“You alone, O bhikkhu, should know by which way you would go to a happy destination.
Then that bhikkhu, stirred by that deity, experienced a sense of spiritual urgency.
The first chapter, the Forest Chapter.
Its summary verse:
Seclusion and attendance, and...
Many [monks] of the Kassapa clan,
Ānanda, Anuruddha,
and Nāgadatta the matron of the household.
Vajjiputta of Vesālī,
through improper recitation,
had his faculties made manifest at midday.
With a lotus flower, one creates fourteen [worlds].
The Connected Discourses on the Forest are completed.
